extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, entomologists, and scientifically-literate readers interested in evolutionary explanations of insect coloration
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and assessing criteria used to infer the evolutionary function(s) of colours and patterns in butterflies, moths, and caterpillars (e.g., protection, display, mimicry, sexual selection). Emphasises empirical signs, behavioural correlates, inheritance patterns, and alternative explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concealment/protective coloration (camouflage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Colours and patterns that render an insect inconspicuous in its usual resting situation (e.g., under-surface resembling a leaf or flower-head; upper surfaces shaded when wings depressed) are adaptive for escaping detection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence includes resemblance of the under surface to surrounding objects (leaf, flower-head), habits of resting with wings depressed or overlapping to hide bright hind-wings, and species that habitually rest motionless being shaded/coloured for escaping detection. Examples: under surface of Iphias glaucippe resembling a pale leaf; many moths' fore-wings concealing hind-wings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Display coloration (visibility for signalling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bright colours specially arranged to be readily seen and exhibited (often by movement or by exposing both wing surfaces) function in display rather than protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diurnal species and those that alternately raise and depress wings (thus exposing both surfaces) are more likely to use colours for display. Lower surfaces sometimes as brightly decorated as uppers; some tropical species have lower surfaces more brilliant. Saturniidae exhibit gentle wing-waving characteristic of display.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sex-limited bright colours imply sexual selection
rubrics_metrics.description: When bright colours are confined chiefly or exclusively to one sex (commonly the male), this pattern is evidence that sexual selection, not protection, produced the coloration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: if a conspicuous colour were protective it should appear in both sexes; male-limited brightness suggests females preferred brighter males and sexual selection operated over generations. Examples: orange-tips present mainly in male Anthocharis; males intensely yellow in Gonepteryx while females paler.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sex-role reversal and female-brightness indicates male choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Where females are the more brilliant sex, this suggests that males selected the more attractive females (i.e., sexual selection acting in reverse).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supportive cases: certain Callidryas species with brighter females; English Thecla and Colias species where females are more ornamented and females take a more active role in supporting males during marriage flight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavioural courtship and rivalry as evidence for sexual selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Prolonged courtship, male-male fights, males crowding around a female, and other active mating behaviours indicate that mate choice can drive the evolution of ornamentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If females prefer one male over another, selection can gradually amplify male traits. Observations: males fighting, pursuing same female, and collectors' reports of pairing behaviour support the plausibility of sexual choice increasing male beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Population sex-ratio and opportunity for mate choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Sex ratios and the relative abundance of the sexes affect which sex will be choosy and thus which sex's appearance will be driven by sexual selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If males are more numerous in the imago state, females can be choosier, favouring brighter males; conversely, if females are more numerous, males may be choosy and select brighter females. The text notes evidence that in many Lepidoptera males exceed females numerically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variability as a prerequisite for sexual selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Sufficient heritable variation in the trait (colour/ornament) within the choosing sex is required for sexual selection to operate and increase beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Papilio childrenae males vary greatly in extent of enamelled green patch and crimson stripe; variability often concentrated in males, facilitating selection. The presence of striking male-to-male variation shows there is material for selection to act upon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inheritance mode affects sex-limited expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Patterns of inheritance (equal inheritance to both sexes vs. inheritance limited to one sex) influence whether ornaments appear in both sexes or only one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equal inheritance tends to transfer male-acquired characters to females; however, sex-limited inheritance (either arising de novo or by selection of sex-limited variants) can allow traits to be expressed in only one sex. Domestication examples show novel characters sometimes appear already sex-limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mimicry: model-abundance and protection of model
rubrics_metrics.description: For Batesian mimicry, the imitated (model) species are abundant and protected (e.g., by distastefulness or odor), while the mimics are relatively rare and co-occur with the model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bates' criteria: imitating species depart from their group's usual colouring, the imitated Heliconidae are conspicuous yet numerous (implying protection), and imitators are rare and live mingled with the models. Empirical confirmation by subsequent observers (Wallace, Trimen, Riley) is cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gradual stepwise evolution of mimicry from similar forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Mimicry likely commenced between forms not widely dissimilar in colour so that even slight beneficial variations made them more like the model; continued gradual change can carry imitators along the model's track.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This addresses the difficulty of how first steps toward mimicry could be advantageous: small initial resemblance suffices and successive variations can accumulate. High propensity for abrupt colour variation in Lepidoptera facilitates this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sex-specific mimicry indicates sex-limited selection/transmission
rubrics_metrics.description: When only one sex (often females) imitates a protected species while the other sex retains ancestral colouring, it indicates selection/transmission has acted primarily on that sex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: cases where females alone imitate brilliant protected species; explanation: variations were transmitted to females alone, possibly because male mimics would be less attractive and thus eliminated by sexual selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bright hind-wings used for predator distraction during flight
rubrics_metrics.description: Hind-wings that are bright yet normally concealed at rest can function as decoys, drawing predator attacks to wings rather than body and allowing escape.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical example: Yellow Under-wings (Triphaena) pursued by birds whose attention is caught by coloured wings; birds strike fragile wing surfaces, enabling moth to escape after losing parts of wings. Wallace's observations on weak flyers with large wings that often escape with pierced wings also support this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlation of diurnal activity and brighter coloration
rubrics_metrics.description: Diurnal Lepidoptera are generally more gaily decorated than nocturnal moths; families that fly by day are often brightly coloured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Families such as Zygaenidae, several Sphingidae, Uraniidae, some Arctiidae and Saturniidae (which fly during day/early evening) are described as extremely beautiful compared with strictly nocturnal kinds. Bright nocturnal exceptions are rare and noteworthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aposematism in caterpillars (warning coloration tied to unpalatability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conspicuously coloured caterpillars may be advertising their unpalatability or unpleasant taste to predators and thus gain protection (aposematism), provided predators can recognise and remember these signals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: tender skin makes caterpillars vulnerable, so distastefulness alone insufficient unless accompanied by a clear outward sign; aviary experiments show birds reject hairy/spiny and some conspicuously-coloured species and show disgust behaviors. Thus gaudy colours would be advantageous if they lead to instant recognition as unpalatable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavioural/habit-based alternative explanations must be considered
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences in colour between sexes might be due to differing habitats or behaviours (e.g., males basking in sun, females in forest), but such explanations are less likely when larval conditions are shared and adult exposure is brief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes male and female larvae are exposed to same conditions, and adult differing conditions are of short duration; hence direct action of different conditions on adult coloration is considered improbable in many cases. Calls for evidence before preferring environmental-dependence over sexual selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ocelli (eye-spots) puzzling for sexual selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Eye-like spots (ocelli) are highly variable and appear ornamental to human eyes, yet they are usually present in both sexes and rarely sexually dimorphic, posing a difficulty for sexual selection explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Potential resolution: if ocellus formation depends on an early developmental tissue change, it may be transmitted to both sexes even if perfected by selection in one sex. Mr. Bates reported ocelli behaviour to Entomological Society; topic flagged as currently inexplicable.
